title: Capitol Reef NP
paragraphs: There is a reef in the Utah desert, hundreds of miles from the nearest ocean. The name comes from two things early travelers saw: white sandstone domes on the skyline that looked like the dome of the U.S. Capitol, and a long wall of cliffs that blocked the way like a reef blocks a ship. That wall is the Waterpocket Fold, a wrinkle in the earth's crust nearly a hundred miles long. Its rock layers buckled upward like a rug draped over a step, then eroded into cliffs, domes and canyons. Fill up in Torrey before you go, because there is no gas inside the park.

The night before I went in, I made camp on the edge of a mesa, with the lights of a faraway town strung along the horizon. The Milky Way poured through a break in the clouds, the trees glowed red, and the tent lit up green like a spaceship that had touched down. In the morning, the road in was all layers. Red cliffs rose over slopes the color of mint ice cream, a fluted maroon mesa wore a cream-colored cap, and a pale haze turned the farthest walls lavender. A gravel road curled past a rock balanced on a hilltop, ready to topple at the next gust of wind. Around Fruita, the Fremont River drew a green line through all that red, and the cottonwoods were a shade of green that looked almost fake in a place this dry! White domes stacked up behind them.

I climbed up out of the valley onto the slickrock, and a striped pyramid of stone appeared between the gnarled trees. From the top of the climb, the whole Fold unrolled: a long red wall running off toward the horizon past a field of pale, rounded domes. At one ledge the ground simply ended, and a thin road lay far below. Those cliffs held hundreds of millions of years, stacked like pages, and I was a bookmark at best.
